Task 18: Heatmap (Hour vs Day of Week)
A heatmap is an excellent way to see two-dimensional patterns. Here we will plot average pedestrian counts by hour of day and day of week.

# Pivot table: hour (rows) x day_of_week (columns)
pivot = ped.pivot_table(
    values="45 Queen Street",
    index="hour",
    columns="day_of_week",
    aggfunc="mean"
)

# Reorder days logically
day_order = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
pivot = pivot[day_order]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
sns.heatmap(pivot, cmap="YlOrRd", annot=True, fmt=".0f", linewidths=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("45 Queen Street: Average Count by Hour and Day", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Hour of Day")
ax.set_xlabel("Day of Week")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








This heatmap reveals the temporal rhythm of the street: strong weekday lunchtime peaks, lower weekend activity, and near-zero counts in the early morning hours.

title: Lab Week 02
text:
What You Have Learnt
This lab covered the complete data analysis workflow from raw CSV to publication-quality figures:

Section 2.1 refreshed your Python fundamentals (variables, lists, loops, conditionals) using Auckland pedestrian sensor data as context.
Section 2.2 introduced pandas DataFrames for reading, exploring, filtering, grouping, reshaping, handling missing data, and merging.
Section 2.3 demonstrated how to create line plots, bar charts, heatmaps, box plots, and multi-panel figures using matplotlib and seaborn.

These skills form the foundation for Section 2.4, where you will add the spatial dimension through GeoPandas, and for the Auckland Footfall Analytics assignment.

title: 2.2. DataFrames and Pandas
text:
Packages and Imports
Before working with pandas, it is worth understanding how Python’s package system works, since you will use import statements at the top of every script from this point onwards.

Installing Packages
Python’s standard library covers the basics, but most data analysis and geospatial work relies on third-party packages. You install them once, then import them into any script that needs them.
# Using uv (recommended for this course)
# uv add pandas

# Using pip
# pip install pandas

# Using conda
# conda install pandas


The import Statement
There are three main ways to bring a package into your code. The first is to import the entire package by name, which requires you to prefix every function call with that name:
import pandas
pandas.read_csv('data.csv')  # Must write "pandas." every time
The second, and most common, is to import with an alias using as. This gives the package a shorter nickname:
import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv('data.csv')  # Shorter and conventional
The third is to import specific items from a package using from, which lets you use them directly without any prefix:
from pathlib import Path
my_path = Path('data/')  # No prefix needed

from math import sqrt, pi
print(sqrt(16))  # 4.0
The from approach is best when you only need one or two items from a package and the names are unambiguous on their own. Avoid from pandas import *, which imports everything into your namespace and makes it unclear where each function comes from.


Standard Aliases
The Python community has settled on conventional aliases for the most common data science packages:
import pandas as pd           # Data manipulation
import numpy as np             # Numerical computing
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # Plotting
import seaborn as sns          # Statistical graphics
import geopandas as gpd        # Geospatial data (Section 2.4)
Using these aliases makes your code instantly readable to other Python users. When you see pd.read_csv() in someone else’s code, you know immediately that it is a pandas function.

title: 2.4. Geospatial Data
section: Reshaping Data with Melt and Pivot
text:
Reshaping Data with Melt and Pivot
Before diving into geospatial analysis, there is one more pandas operation that proves indispensable when preparing data for spatial visualisation: reshaping between wide and long formats. The melt() function converts a wide DataFrame (where each variable occupies its own column) into a long format (where variable names become values in a single column). The inverse operation, pivot(), converts long data back to wide.
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'City': ['Auckland', 'Wellington', 'Christchurch'],
    'Jan_Temp': [25, 22, 20],
    'Feb_Temp': [24, 21, 19],
    'Mar_Temp': [23, 20, 18]
})

print("Original DataFrame:")
print(df)

# Using melt to reshape the DataFrame
df_melted = pd.melt(
    df,
    id_vars=['City'],
    var_name='Month',
    value_name='Temperature'
)

print("\nMelted DataFrame:")
print(df_melted)
The id_vars parameter specifies which columns should remain as identifiers (i.e. they stay as columns), while all remaining columns are “unpivoted” into two new columns: one for the variable names (var_name) and one for their values (value_name). This long format is essential for many plotting libraries such as seaborn, which expect data in tidy (long) format.
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set(style="whitegrid")

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.lineplot(
    data=df_melted,
    x='Month',
    y='Temperature',
    hue='City',
    marker='o'
)

plt.title('Monthly Temperatures Across Cities', fontsize=16)
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Temperature (°C)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.legend(title='City')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 2.4. Geospatial Data
text:
Vector Tools
Vector tools are the core spatial operations for manipulating discrete geographic features. The most commonly used operations are:

Buffer: creates a zone around a feature at a defined distance, useful for proximity analysis
Clip: extracts a specific area from one dataset using another dataset as a boundary
Dissolve: merges multiple features into one based on a common attribute
Difference (Erase): removes areas of one layer that overlap with another
Intersect: extracts overlapping portions of two layers
Merge: combines two or more layers into one
Spatial Join: matches features based on their relative spatial locations


Vector Tools in Python
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Polygon, Point, LineString

gdf.buffer(distance)                         # Buffer
gpd.clip(gdf, mask)                          # Clip
gpd.overlay(A, B, how='difference')          # Difference (Erase)
gdf.dissolve(by='region')                    # Dissolve
gpd.overlay(A, B, how='intersection')        # Intersect


Buffering Example
# Reproject to a metric CRS
cities_3857 = cities.to_crs(epsg=3857)

# Create a copy and add a 250km buffer around all cities
buffered_cities = cities_3857.copy()
buffered_cities["geometry"] = buffered_cities.buffer(250e3)


Overlay Example: Difference
africa = countries.loc[countries["continent"] == "Africa"]
africa = africa.to_crs(epsg=3857)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

# Calculate the difference of the geometry sets
diff = gpd.overlay(africa, buffered_cities, how="difference")

diff.plot(facecolor="#b9f2b1", ax=ax)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_aspect("equal")


Dissolve Example
# Dissolve NZ regions by island
dissolved = pop23.dissolve(by='Island').reset_index()
dissolved.plot(column='Island')

title: 2.4. Geospatial Data
text:
Raster Data Analysis
So far we have been working mainly with vector data using geopandas. Raster data is the other major geospatial data type: gridded or pixelated data that maps naturally to arrays.

Raster Characteristics
Raster datasets have two key properties. Resolution is the spatial distance that a single pixel covers on the ground: higher resolution means smaller pixels and more detail. Extent is the bounding box that covers the entire spatial footprint of the dataset.
Raster data can be continuous (multispectral satellite imagery, digital elevation models, canopy height from LiDAR) or categorical (land cover maps, snowcover masks).


Multi-band Raster Data
Colour images are multi-band rasters, where each band measures light reflected from a different part of the electromagnetic spectrum (e.g. red, green, blue, near-infrared). The standard raster format is GeoTIFF, a .tif file with embedded spatial metadata including geotransform (extent, resolution), CRS, and NoData values.


Working with rasterio
import rasterio as rio

elev = rio.open('nz_elev.tif')
elev.crs          # Coordinate reference system
elev.bounds       # Spatial extent
elev.count        # Number of bands
elev.indexes      # Band numbers available
elev.shape        # Pixel dimensions (rows, cols)
elev.meta         # All metadata


Common Raster Operations
Slope identifies the steepness at each cell of a raster surface using a moving window (typically 3x3). Lower slope values indicate flatter terrain; higher values indicate steeper terrain.
Mask raster by vector boundaries clips a raster to the extent of a vector boundary, useful for extracting raster values within a study area.
Zonal statistics calculates summary statistics (mean, sum, count, etc.) on raster cell values within zones defined by a vector dataset.

text:
Questions to Think About
Now that you have produced the maps, take some time to reflect on the patterns. Discuss these with your lab partner or write short answers in your notebook.






Q1: Spatial Shift Through the Day



Compare the 7 am and 5 pm maps. Does the “centre of gravity” of pedestrian activity shift location between morning and evening? In which direction, and why?








Q2: Morning vs Evening Symmetry



Are the 7 am and 7 pm maps roughly symmetrical (similar numbers but reversed in time), or do they look different? What might explain any asymmetry?








Q3: Lunchtime Hotspots



At 1 pm, which sensors show the highest counts? Are these the same sensors that dominate at 5 pm? What does this tell you about the difference between lunchtime foot traffic and commuter foot traffic?








Q4: Waterfront vs Queen Street



Compare the Quay Street sensors (waterfront) with the Queen Street sensors (retail corridor). Do they follow the same daily pattern, or do they peak at different times? What urban functions might explain the difference?








Q5: K Road vs CBD Core



The K Road sensors (150 and 183 K Road) are roughly 1.5 km south of the CBD core. How do their counts compare in absolute terms? Do they peak at the same hour as the CBD sensors?








Q6: Aggregation Choices



We averaged across all 31 days in March. How might the maps change if you:

Used median instead of mean?
Separated weekdays from weekends?
Chose different hours (e.g. 8 am instead of 7 am)?









Q7: Data Limitations



The sensors only capture 21 locations. How representative are these of pedestrian activity across the entire CBD? What additional data sources might help fill the gaps?

section: Step 7: Web Map with Sized Circles
text:
Step 7: Web Map with Sized Circles
The .explore() map uses the same dot size for every sensor. We can use the folium library to draw circles whose size reflects the pedestrian count, making busy sensors visually larger.

import folium

# Create a base map centred on Auckland CBD
m = folium.Map(
    location=[-36.849, 174.765],
    zoom_start=15,
    tiles="CartoDB positron"
)

# Filter to 5 pm
hour_17 = gdf[gdf["hour"] == 17]

# Add a circle for each sensor.
# Don't worry about this loop syntax for now -- just run it!
# It goes through each sensor one at a time and places a circle on the map.
for _, row in hour_17.iterrows():
    folium.CircleMarker(
        location=[row["Latitude"], row["Longitude"]],
        radius=row["avg_count"] / 80,       # bigger count = bigger circle
        color="black",
        weight=0.5,
        fill=True,
        fill_color="red",
        fill_opacity=0.6,
        tooltip=f"{row['Address']}: {int(row['avg_count'])} avg/hr"
    ).add_to(m)

title: Lab Week 04
text:
About OSMnx
OSMnx is a Python library that downloads street network data from OpenStreetMap and converts it into a NetworkX graph. We can then extract nodes (intersections and dead ends) and edges (street segments) as GeoDataFrames for spatial analysis.

title: Lab Week 04
section: Task 1: Downloading the Auckland CBD Network
text:
Task 1: Downloading the Auckland CBD Network

import osmnx as ox
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Download the walkable street network for Auckland CBD
# network_type='walk' includes footpaths, pedestrian streets, and shared paths
# We use a bounding box centred on the CBD to capture the sensor area
G = ox.graph_from_bbox(
    bbox=(-36.839, -36.862, 174.755, 174.775),
    network_type='walk'
)

print(f"Nodes (intersections): {G.number_of_nodes()}")
print(f"Edges (street segments): {G.number_of_edges()}")


# Convert the graph to GeoDataFrames
nodes, edges = ox.graph_to_gdfs(G)

print(f"Nodes shape: {nodes.shape}")
print(f"Edges shape: {edges.shape}")


# Inspect the nodes table
nodes.head()


# Inspect the edges table
edges.head()

Each node has a latitude, longitude, and geometry (point). Each edge has a length in metres, a geometry (linestring), and street attributes such as name and highway type.
Your turn: How many unique street names appear in the edges table? Use edges["name"].nunique() (you may need to handle lists first). Are there any unnamed segments?

fig, ax = ox.plot_graph(

Place Name Alternative

G = ox.graph_from_place("Auckland, New Zealand", network_type='walk')
You can also use ox.graph_from_point() with a distance radius:
G = ox.graph_from_point((-36.849, 174.765), dist=1000, network_type='walk')


Your turn: Try downloading the network with network_type='drive' instead. How does the number of edges change? Why might the walkable network have more edges than the drivable one?

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 3: Node Degree
Node degree is the number of street segments meeting at an intersection. A 4-way intersection has degree 4; a dead end has degree 1. Higher average degree indicates a more connected, grid-like network with more route choices for pedestrians.

import momepy

# Calculate node degree
# momepy expects the graph as a NetworkX object
degree_dict = dict(G.degree())

# Add degree to the nodes GeoDataFrame
nodes["degree"] = nodes.index.map(degree_dict)

print(f"Average node degree: {nodes['degree'].mean():.2f}")
print(f"Maximum degree: {nodes['degree'].max()}")
print(f"Minimum degree: {nodes['degree'].min()}")


# Distribution of node degrees
print(nodes["degree"].value_counts().sort_index())


# Map node degree
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))

nodes.plot(
    ax=ax,
    column="degree",
    cmap="YlOrRd",
    markersize=nodes["degree"] * 8,
    edgecolor="black",
    linewidth=0.3,
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Node Degree", "shrink": 0.6}
)

edges.plot(ax=ax, color="#cccccc", linewidth=0.3, zorder=0)

ax.set_title("Auckland CBD: Node Degree (Street Connectivity)", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







What Does Node Degree Tell Us?



A node with degree 1 is a dead end. Degree 2 means the street simply continues (no intersection). Degree 3 is a T-junction, and degree 4 is a standard crossroads. Nodes with degree 5 or higher are complex intersections with many route choices. For walkability, higher average degree generally means a more permeable network.


Your turn: What percentage of nodes are dead ends (degree 1)? What percentage are crossroads or higher (degree >= 4)?

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 4: Closeness Centrality
Closeness centrality measures how close a node is to all other nodes in the network. A node with high closeness centrality can be reached from anywhere in the network with relatively short travel distances. This is a proxy for accessibility.

import networkx as nx

# Calculate closeness centrality using network distance (edge length)
centrality = nx.closeness_centrality(G, distance="length")

# Add to nodes GeoDataFrame
nodes["closeness"] = nodes.index.map(centrality)

print(f"Mean closeness centrality: {nodes['closeness'].mean():.6f}")
print(f"Max closeness centrality: {nodes['closeness'].max():.6f}")
print(f"Min closeness centrality: {nodes['closeness'].min():.6f}")


# Map closeness centrality
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))

nodes.plot(
    ax=ax,
    column="closeness",
    cmap="plasma",
    markersize=15,
    edgecolor="none",
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Closeness Centrality", "shrink": 0.6}
)

edges.plot(ax=ax, color="#cccccc", linewidth=0.3, zorder=0)

ax.set_title("Auckland CBD: Closeness Centrality", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Your turn: Which area of the CBD has the highest closeness centrality? Does this align with where you would expect the most accessible location to be?

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 5: Betweenness Centrality
Betweenness centrality measures how often a node lies on the shortest path between other pairs of nodes. A node with high betweenness is a critical route through the network. Removing it would force pedestrians to take longer detours.

# Calculate betweenness centrality (may take a moment)
betweenness = nx.betweenness_centrality(G, weight="length")

nodes["betweenness"] = nodes.index.map(betweenness)

print(f"Mean betweenness: {nodes['betweenness'].mean():.6f}")
print(f"Max betweenness: {nodes['betweenness'].max():.6f}")


# Map betweenness centrality
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))

nodes.plot(
    ax=ax,
    column="betweenness",
    cmap="inferno",
    markersize=15,
    edgecolor="none",
    legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Betweenness Centrality", "shrink": 0.6}
)

edges.plot(ax=ax, color="#cccccc", linewidth=0.3, zorder=0)

ax.set_title("Auckland CBD: Betweenness Centrality", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Closeness vs Betweenness



Closeness centrality answers “how easy is it to reach everywhere from here?” whilst betweenness centrality answers “how many shortest paths pass through here?” A node can be highly central by closeness but low by betweenness if it is well-located but not on many through-routes. Both are useful for understanding pedestrian flow patterns.


Your turn: Create a side-by-side comparison (1 x 2 subplot) of closeness and betweenness centrality maps. Do the spatial patterns differ?

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 6: Network Summary Statistics
Momepy and NetworkX together provide several summary statistics that characterise the overall walkability of a street network.

# Basic network statistics from OSMnx
stats = ox.stats.basic_stats(G)

print("=== Network Summary ===")
print(f"Number of nodes:        {stats['n']}")
print(f"Number of edges:        {stats['m']}")
print(f"Average node degree:    {stats['k_avg']:.2f}")
print(f"Total edge length:      {stats['edge_length_total']:.0f} m")
print(f"Average edge length:    {stats['edge_length_avg']:.1f} m")


# Intersection count (nodes with degree > 1)
intersections = nodes[nodes["degree"] > 1]
dead_ends = nodes[nodes["degree"] == 1]

print(f"\nIntersections:          {len(intersections)}")
print(f"Dead ends:              {len(dead_ends)}")
print(f"Dead-end ratio:         {len(dead_ends) / len(nodes):.1%}")


# Meshedness ratio: proportion of actual loops relative to maximum possible
# A higher meshedness means more route choices
n_nodes = G.number_of_nodes()
n_edges = G.number_of_edges()
meshedness = (n_edges - n_nodes + 1) / (2 * n_nodes - 5) if n_nodes > 2 else 0

print(f"\nMeshedness ratio:       {meshedness:.3f}")
print("(0 = tree/no loops, 1 = maximally connected)")







Interpreting Meshedness



A meshedness ratio close to 0 means the network is tree-like with few alternative routes. A ratio closer to 1 means there are many loops and route choices. Most urban street networks fall between 0.1 and 0.5. Higher values generally indicate better walkability because pedestrians have more route options.


Your turn: Compare the meshedness of the walk network with the drive network. Which is more “meshed” and why?

title: Lab Week 04
section: Task 7: Loading and Preparing the Pedestrian Data
text:
Task 7: Loading and Preparing the Pedestrian Data

# Load pedestrian counts and geodata
ped = pd.read_csv("data/akl_ped-2024.csv")
geo = pd.read_csv("data/akl_ped-Geodata.csv")

# Clean the pedestrian data
ped = ped.dropna(subset=["Date", "Time"]).copy()
ped = ped[ped["Date"] != "Daylight Savings"].copy()
ped["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(ped["Date"])

# Extract temporal features
ped["hour"] = ped["Time"].str.split(":").str[0].astype(int)
ped["month"] = ped["Date"].dt.month

# Sensor columns
sensor_cols = ped.columns[2:23]

print(f"Pedestrian data: {ped.shape}")
print(f"Sensor locations: {len(geo)}")


# Calculate the annual average hourly count for each sensor
avg_counts = ped[sensor_cols].mean()

# Create a summary table with coordinates
sensor_summary = geo.copy()
sensor_summary["avg_count"] = sensor_summary["Address"].map(avg_counts)
sensor_summary = sensor_summary.dropna(subset=["avg_count"])

print("Average hourly count by sensor:")
print(sensor_summary[["Address", "avg_count"]].sort_values("avg_count", ascending=False).to_string(index=False))

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 8: Creating a Spatial Join
To link pedestrian sensors with network nodes, we need to find the nearest node to each sensor location. This requires projecting both datasets to a metric coordinate reference system (NZGD2000 / New Zealand Transverse Mercator, EPSG:2193).

# Convert sensors to GeoDataFrame
sensor_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    sensor_summary,
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(sensor_summary["Longitude"], sensor_summary["Latitude"]),
    crs="EPSG:4326"
)

# Project both to NZTM (metres)
sensor_proj = sensor_gdf.to_crs("EPSG:2193")
nodes_proj = nodes.to_crs("EPSG:2193")

print(f"Sensors: {len(sensor_proj)}")
print(f"Network nodes: {len(nodes_proj)}")


# Find the nearest network node for each sensor
from shapely.ops import nearest_points

def find_nearest_node(sensor_point, nodes_gdf):
    """Return the index of the nearest node to a given point."""
    distances = nodes_gdf.geometry.distance(sensor_point)
    nearest_idx = distances.idxmin()
    return nearest_idx, distances[nearest_idx]

# Apply to each sensor
results = sensor_proj.geometry.apply(lambda pt: find_nearest_node(pt, nodes_proj))
sensor_proj["nearest_node"] = results.apply(lambda x: x[0])
sensor_proj["distance_to_node"] = results.apply(lambda x: x[1])

print("Distance from each sensor to its nearest node (metres):")
print(sensor_proj[["Address", "distance_to_node"]].to_string(index=False))


# Join morphological measures from nodes to sensors
sensor_morphology = sensor_proj.merge(
    nodes[["degree", "closeness", "betweenness"]],
    left_on="nearest_node",
    right_index=True,
    how="left"
)

sensor_morphology[["Address", "avg_count", "degree", "closeness", "betweenness"]].round(6)







Spatial Join Caveats



We have only 19 sensor locations, which is a small sample for correlation analysis. The nearest node may not perfectly represent the morphological context of the sensor (a sensor on a long block might be far from the nearest intersection). Interpret results as exploratory rather than confirmatory.


Your turn: Check the distance_to_node values. Are any sensors suspiciously far from their nearest node? How might you set a maximum threshold (e.g. 100 m) to filter out poor matches?

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Task 9: Testing the Hypothesis

from scipy.stats import pearsonr, spearmanr

# Pearson correlation: degree vs average footfall
corr_degree, p_degree = pearsonr(
    sensor_morphology["degree"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

# Spearman correlation (rank-based, less sensitive to outliers)
rho_degree, p_rho_degree = spearmanr(
    sensor_morphology["degree"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

print("=== Degree vs Pedestrian Count ===")
print(f"Pearson r  = {corr_degree:.3f}  (p = {p_degree:.3f})")
print(f"Spearman ρ = {rho_degree:.3f}  (p = {p_rho_degree:.3f})")


# Closeness centrality vs footfall
corr_close, p_close = pearsonr(
    sensor_morphology["closeness"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

rho_close, p_rho_close = spearmanr(
    sensor_morphology["closeness"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

print("=== Closeness Centrality vs Pedestrian Count ===")
print(f"Pearson r  = {corr_close:.3f}  (p = {p_close:.3f})")
print(f"Spearman ρ = {rho_close:.3f}  (p = {p_rho_close:.3f})")


# Betweenness centrality vs footfall
corr_btwn, p_btwn = pearsonr(
    sensor_morphology["betweenness"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

rho_btwn, p_rho_btwn = spearmanr(
    sensor_morphology["betweenness"],
    sensor_morphology["avg_count"]
)

print("=== Betweenness Centrality vs Pedestrian Count ===")
print(f"Pearson r  = {corr_btwn:.3f}  (p = {p_btwn:.3f})")
print(f"Spearman ρ = {rho_btwn:.3f}  (p = {p_rho_btwn:.3f})")







Interpreting the Results



A positive correlation means that sensors near more connected/central nodes tend to have higher pedestrian counts. A p-value below 0.05 is conventionally considered statistically significant, but with only 19 observations, treat significance cautiously. The Spearman rank correlation is more robust when the relationship is not strictly linear or when outliers are present.


Your turn: Does the correlation change if you use only weekday data (Monday to Friday)? Recalculate avg_count for weekdays only and re-run the correlation tests.

title: Lab Week 04
section: Task 13: Temporal Variation in Form-Function Relationship
text:
Task 13: Temporal Variation in Form-Function Relationship
Does the relationship between urban form and pedestrian activity change throughout the day? During the morning rush, commuters may follow direct routes (favouring high-betweenness nodes), whilst at lunchtime, pedestrians may disperse to a wider variety of destinations.

# Calculate average counts by hour for each sensor
target_hours = [7, 9, 12, 15, 17, 20]

hourly_correlations = []

for h in target_hours:
    hour_data = ped[ped["hour"] == h][sensor_cols].mean()

    # Match to sensors with morphology data
    temp = sensor_morphology.copy()
    temp["hour_count"] = temp["Address"].map(hour_data)
    temp = temp.dropna(subset=["hour_count"])

    r_degree, _ = pearsonr(temp["degree"], temp["hour_count"])
    r_close, _ = pearsonr(temp["closeness"], temp["hour_count"])
    r_btwn, _ = pearsonr(temp["betweenness"], temp["hour_count"])

    hourly_correlations.append({
        "hour": h,
        "r_degree": r_degree,
        "r_closeness": r_close,
        "r_betweenness": r_btwn
    })

corr_df = pd.DataFrame(hourly_correlations)
print(corr_df.round(3))


# Plot how correlations change through the day
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

ax.plot(corr_df["hour"], corr_df["r_degree"], "o-", label="Node Degree", color="#1C7293", linewidth=2)
ax.plot(corr_df["hour"], corr_df["r_closeness"], "s-", label="Closeness", color="#F96167", linewidth=2)
ax.plot(corr_df["hour"], corr_df["r_betweenness"], "^-", label="Betweenness", color="#1B998B", linewidth=2)

ax.axhline(y=0, color="grey", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Hour of Day")
ax.set_ylabel("Pearson Correlation (r)")
ax.set_title("How Does the Form-Function Relationship Change Through the Day?", fontweight="bold")
ax.legend()
ax.set_xticks(target_hours)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{h}:00" for h in target_hours])
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Your turn: Extend this analysis to compare weekdays and weekends. Do the correlations differ? You might expect betweenness to matter more on weekdays (commuters taking efficient routes) and closeness to matter more on weekends (leisure pedestrians exploring).

title: Lab Week 04
text:
What is an API?
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that lets your code talk to a remote server and request data. Instead of downloading a file manually from a website, you send a structured request to a URL and receive structured data back. This is the foundation of reproducible data acquisition: your script is the download step.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Downloading Earthquake Data
We begin with the simplest possible API example. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) publishes a real-time feed of recent earthquakes as GeoJSON. Because geopandas can read GeoJSON directly from a URL, a single line of code is enough to turn this feed into a spatial dataframe.
The USGS earthquake feed at earthquake.usgs.gov returns all magnitude 2.5+ earthquakes from the past seven days.

import geopandas as gpd

# Download data on magnitude 2.5+ quakes from the past week
endpoint_url = (
     "http://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/feed/v1.0/summary/2.5_week.geojson"
 )
earthquakes = gpd.read_file(endpoint_url)
print(earthquakes.head())

That is the entire script. The key insight is that the USGS server returns a GeoJSON FeatureCollection, which is a format that GeoPandas understands natively. No authentication is required for this feed.






Try it yourself



Run the code above and inspect the resulting dataframe. What columns are available? Try plotting the earthquakes on a world map with earthquakes.plot(). You can also colour the points by magnitude: earthquakes.plot(column="mag", cmap="OrRd", legend=True).

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Understanding the Pattern
Even though this example is short, it demonstrates the core API pattern that we will use throughout this lab:







Step
What happens




1. Construct a URL
The URL encodes what you want (earthquake data, magnitude 2.5+, past week)


2. Send a request
gpd.read_file() sends an HTTP GET request to the server


3. Parse the response
The GeoJSON response is automatically converted to a GeoDataFrame



In Parts 2 and 3, we will see how to add query parameters, authentication, and more complex workflows, but the fundamental pattern remains the same.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 1: Query the API
Unlike the USGS feed, the CARTO API takes query parameters. We pass a SQL query (q), the output format (format), and optionally which fields to skip.

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import requests
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

pd.options.display.max_columns = 999

# The API endpoint
carto_api_endpoint = "https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql"

# The query parameters
params = {
    "q": "SELECT * FROM shootings",
    "format": "geojson",
    "skipfields": "cartodb_id",
}

response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)
response







SQL via API



The CARTO SQL API is powerful because it lets you run arbitrary SQL queries on the server side. This means you can filter and aggregate data before downloading it, reducing both bandwidth and processing time on your local machine.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 2: Parse the Response
The response is a GeoJSON dictionary. We can inspect its structure and then convert it to a GeoDataFrame.

# Get the returned data in JSON format
# This is a dictionary
features = response.json()
type(features)

# What are the keys?
list(features.keys())

# Let's look at the first feature
features["features"][0]

# Create a GeoDataFrame
shootings = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(features, crs="EPSG:4326")
shootings.head()

text:
Step 3: Clean and Project

# Make sure we remove missing geometries
shootings = shootings.dropna(subset=["geometry"])

# Convert to a better CRS
shootings = shootings.to_crs(epsg=3857)

# Load city limits to clip the data
city_limits = gpd.read_file(
    "https://opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/405ec3da942d4e20869d4e1449a2be48_0.geojson"
).to_crs(epsg=3857)

# Remove any shootings that are outside the city limits
shootings = gpd.sjoin(
    shootings, city_limits, predicate="within", how="inner"
).drop(columns=["index_right"])

Step 4: Visualisation
With the cleaned data in hand, we can produce two complementary visualisations: a point map and a hexbin map.

    "https://opendata.arcgis.com/datasets/b54ec5210cee41c3a884c9086f7af1be_0.geojson"

Hexbin Map
A hexbin map aggregates point events into hexagonal bins, revealing density patterns that are hard to see in a simple point map.

# Initialize the axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10), facecolor=plt.get_cmap("viridis")(0))

# Convert to Web Mercator and plot the hexbins
x = shootings.geometry.x
y = shootings.geometry.y
ax.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=40, mincnt=1, cmap="viridis")

# Overlay the city limits
zip_codes.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="none", linewidth=0.5, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_axis_off()

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Step 5: Filtering with SQL
One of the strengths of the CARTO API is that you can filter on the server side using SQL.

# Example: Count the total number of rows in a table
response = requests.get(
    carto_api_endpoint, params={"q": "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shootings"}
)
response.json()

# Select nonfatal shootings only
query = "SELECT * FROM shootings WHERE fatal = 0"
params = {"q": query, "format": "geojson"}
response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)

# Make the GeoDataFrame
nonfatal = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(response.json(), crs="EPSG:4326")
print("number of nonfatal shootings = ", len(nonfatal))

# Select based on "date_"
query = "SELECT * FROM shootings WHERE date_ >= '1/1/23'"
params = {"q": query, "format": "geojson"}
response = requests.get(carto_api_endpoint, params=params)

# Make the GeoDataFrame
shootings_2023 = gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(response.json(), crs="EPSG:4326")
print("number of shootings in 2023 = ", len(shootings_2023))

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Introduction
This part introduces two programmatic methods for downloading GIS layers from New Zealand’s national spatial data services: the Stats NZ Geographic Data Service (datafinder.stats.govt.nz) and the LINZ Data Service (data.linz.govt.nz). Rather than clicking through the web interface every time, you will write Python scripts that fetch, poll, and load geospatial data automatically. This is an essential habit in reproducible research: when your data acquisition step is scripted, anyone can re-run your entire workflow from scratch.
Both services are built on the Koordinates platform, which exposes a REST API. Every dataset you can browse in the web interface is also accessible programmatically using either of the two methods below.






Why programmatic download?



A manual download is fine for a one-off task, but it breaks reproducibility. If you are sharing your analysis through GitHub, a Quarto report, or a package, your collaborators cannot re-run the data acquisition step unless the exact same file is committed to the repository (which is impractical for large GIS files). A short script that downloads the data on demand is far more transparent and maintainable.



Methods covered








Method
Approach
Best for




Method A
Koordinates Export API
Saving a local GeoPackage or Shapefile; offline workflows


Method B
WFS (Web Feature Service)
Loading directly into a GeoDataFrame; spatial subsetting with a bounding box

section: Step 1: Create an Account and Obtain an API Key
text:
Step 1: Create an Account and Obtain an API Key
Both methods require a personal API key. Navigate to the Stats NZ Geographic Data Service and log in using your Koordinates ID. If you do not yet have one, click Sign Up on the login page.



Log in to Stats NZ Geographic Data Service using your Koordinates ID. If you do not have an account, click Sign Up to register.


Once logged in, go to:

https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/my/api/

Click Create API Key, give it a descriptive name (for example, GISCI343), and copy the key value. You will not be shown the full key again after navigating away from the page.






Keep your API key private



Your API key is a credential. Treat it like a password. Never paste it directly into a shared notebook or commit it to a public repository.
Store it in a separate file (for example config.py) that is listed in your .gitignore:

title: Lab Week 04
section: Step 2: Find the Layer You Need
text:
Step 2: Find the Layer You Need
For this lab we will use the Regional Council 2025 Clipped layer (Layer ID: 120945), which contains the 17 regional boundaries of New Zealand.
Navigate to the layer page to review the metadata before downloading:

https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/layer/120945-regional-council-2025-clipped/

The homepage provides a search bar and a catalogue of all available datasets:



Stats NZ Geographic Data Service homepage — search for a dataset by name, or browse the Most Popular section.



Finding the Layer ID
Every API request requires the Layer ID, the integer that uniquely identifies a dataset. There are two ways to find it.
Method 1: Read it from the URL
When you open any layer page, the Layer ID is embedded directly in the browser address bar:
https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/layer/120945-regional-council-2025-clipped/
                                       ^^^^^^
                                       This is the Layer ID
Method 2: Read it from the Info tab
Open the layer page and make sure the Info tab is selected (it is the default). Scroll down below the thumbnail and you will see a metadata row showing Date Added, Last Updated, Views, Exports, and Layer ID. The number displayed there (e.g. 120945) is what you use in your script.



Two places the Layer ID appears: highlighted in the URL bar (top) and in the metadata row of the Info tab (bottom left).








Quick tip: search first, then check the URL



Search for the dataset you need using the search bar on the homepage. Once you have opened the correct layer page, copy the integer from the URL. It is always the first numeric segment after /layer/. You do not need to navigate anywhere else.

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Method A: Koordinates Export API
The Export API creates a downloadable ZIP archive of a layer in a format and CRS of your choice. The workflow has three stages: create, poll, then download.
The settings you choose when calling the API mirror exactly what the web interface shows in the Export dialog:



Export dialog — the CRS dropdown, format selector, and layer checkbox correspond directly to the fields in the API request body.



Stage 1: Create the Export Job
Send a POST request with a JSON body specifying the layer URL, CRS, and file format. The Authorization header carries your API key.

import requests
import time
import zipfile
import io
import geopandas as gpd

from config import API_KEY  # store your key in config.py

LAYER_ID = 120945
BASE_URL = "https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/services/api/v1.x"

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"key {API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type":  "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "crs":     "EPSG:2193",
    "formats": {"vector": "application/x-ogc-gpkg"},
    "items":   [{"item": f"{BASE_URL}/layers/{LAYER_ID}/"}],
}

response = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/exports/", json=payload, headers=HEADERS)
response.raise_for_status()

export_data = response.json()
export_url  = export_data["url"]
print(f"Export job created: {export_url}")
print(f"Current state: {export_data['state']}")







Available format strings






Format string
Output




application/x-ogc-gpkg
GeoPackage (recommended)


application/x-zipped-shp
Shapefile (ZIP)


application/json
GeoJSON


text/csv
CSV (attributes only, no geometry)







Stage 2: Poll Until Ready
The export is prepared asynchronously. Check the state field every few seconds until it returns "complete".

print("Waiting for export...", end="", flush=True)

while True:
    poll = requests.get(export_url, headers=HEADERS)
    poll.raise_for_status()
    state = poll.json()["state"]
    print(".", end="", flush=True)

    if state == "complete":
        download_url = poll.json()["download_url"]
        print(f"\nReady: {download_url}")
        break
    elif state in ("error", "cancelled"):
        raise RuntimeError(f"Export failed with state: {state}")

    time.sleep(5)



Stage 3: Download and Load
You can either save the ZIP to disk first, or extract it entirely in memory.

# --- Option 1: Save to disk ---
dl = requests.get(download_url, headers=HEADERS, stream=True)
dl.raise_for_status()

with open("regional_council_2025.zip", "wb") as f:
    for chunk in dl.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
        f.write(chunk)

with zipfile.ZipFile("regional_council_2025.zip") as zf:
    gpkg_name = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".gpkg")][0]
    zf.extractall("regional_council_2025/")

gdf = gpd.read_file(f"regional_council_2025/{gpkg_name}")
print(gdf.shape, gdf.crs)


# --- Option 2: Extract entirely in memory (no file saved) ---
dl2 = requests.get(download_url, headers=HEADERS)
with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(dl2.content)) as zf:
    gpkg_name = [n for n in zf.namelist() if n.endswith(".gpkg")][0]
    gdf = gpd.read_file(zf.open(gpkg_name))

print(gdf.shape, gdf.crs)
gdf.plot()

title: Lab Week 04
text:
Method B: WFS (Web Feature Service)
WFS is an OGC standard that lets you stream vector features directly into Python without downloading a ZIP. The endpoint is found under the Services and APIs tab on the layer page. Select WFS from the left-hand list and choose your API key from the dropdown.



Services and APIs tab — click WFS in the left panel to see the pre-filled endpoint URL and API key selector.



Read Directly into a GeoDataFrame
Construct the WFS URL and pass it directly to gpd.read_file(). GeoPandas fetches and parses the GeoJSON response automatically.

import geopandas as gpd
from config import API_KEY

LAYER_ID = 120945
wfs_base = f"https://datafinder.stats.govt.nz/services;key={API_KEY}/wfs/"

params = (
    "service=WFS&version=2.0.0&request=GetFeature"
    f"&typeNames=layer-{LAYER_ID}"
    "&outputFormat=application/json"
    "&srsName=EPSG:2193"
)

gdf = gpd.read_file(f"{wfs_base}?{params}")
print(gdf.shape)   # (17, n_columns)
print(gdf.crs)     # EPSG:2193
gdf.plot(figsize=(8, 10))



Spatial Subsetting with a Bounding Box
For large layers, add a bbox parameter to retrieve only the features intersecting a defined area:

# Bounding box for Auckland region (EPSG:2193, metres)
# Format: min_easting, min_northing, max_easting, max_northing
bbox = "1730000,5900000,1820000,5990000"

params_bbox = (
    "service=WFS&version=2.0.0&request=GetFeature"
    f"&typeNames=layer-{LAYER_ID}"
    "&outputFormat=application/json&srsName=EPSG:2193"
    f"&bbox={bbox},EPSG:2193"
)

gdf_akl = gpd.read_file(f"{wfs_base}?{params_bbox}")
print(gdf_akl[["REGC2025_1", "LAND_AREA_SQ_KM"]])
gdf_akl.plot(figsize=(6, 6))







When should you use the bbox parameter?



The Regional Council layer only has 17 features, so bbox filtering saves little time here. However, for large layers such as meshblocks (~50,000 features) or building outlines (~3 million features), restricting to your study area makes a significant difference in download time and memory usage.

title: Lab Week 04
section: Applying the Same Methods to LINZ Data Service
text:
Applying the Same Methods to LINZ Data Service
The LINZ Data Service (data.linz.govt.nz) also runs on the Koordinates platform. This means the same two methods (Export API and WFS) work with only minor changes. You will need a separate API key from LINZ: sign up at data.linz.govt.nz, then go to My Account > API Keys and generate one.
In this section we will download NZ Building Outlines (All Sources) (Layer ID: 101292) and plot the results for Auckland city centre.

https://data.linz.govt.nz/layer/101292-nz-building-outlines-all-sources/







Large layers require spatial filtering



The NZ Building Outlines layer contains approximately 3 million features nationally. Downloading the full layer via WFS is impractical. Always use a bounding box or the Export API when working with large datasets like this.



LINZ WFS with Bounding Box
The LINZ WFS endpoint uses cql_filter with a bbox() function for spatial filtering, rather than the standard WFS bbox parameter. The geometry column for most LINZ layers is called shape.

import json
import requests
import geopandas as gpd
from config import LINZ_API_KEY  # store separately from Stats NZ key

LAYER_ID = 101292
WFS_URL = f"https://data.linz.govt.nz/services;key={LINZ_API_KEY}/wfs"

# Auckland city centre bounding box (EPSG:4326)
# min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat
BBOX = (174.7339, -36.8679, 174.8013, -36.8284)

params = {
    "service": "WFS",
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "request": "GetFeature",
    "typeNames": f"layer-{LAYER_ID}",
    "outputFormat": "application/json",
    "srsName": "EPSG:4326",
    "count": 50000,
    "cql_filter": (
        f"bbox(shape,{BBOX[0]},{BBOX[1]},{BBOX[2]},{BBOX[3]},'EPSG:4326')"
    ),
}

response = requests.get(WFS_URL, params=params, timeout=300)
response.raise_for_status()

geojson = response.json()
n_features = len(geojson.get("features", []))
print(f"Received {n_features} building outlines.")

# Save to file
with open("auckland_cbd_buildings.geojson", "w") as f:
    json.dump(geojson, f, indent=2)







Key differences between Stats NZ and LINZ WFS











Feature
Stats NZ
LINZ




Base URL
datafinder.stats.govt.nz
data.linz.govt.nz


API key
Stats NZ Koordinates account
LINZ Koordinates account


Spatial filter
Standard WFS bbox parameter
cql_filter=bbox(shape,...)


Default CRS
EPSG:2193 (NZTM)
EPSG:2193 (NZTM)







Plotting the Auckland City Centre Buildings
Once downloaded, load the GeoJSON into a GeoDataFrame and plot with a basemap for geographic context. The contextily library adds background map tiles automatically.

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

try:
    import contextily as cx
    HAS_BASEMAP = True
except ImportError:
    HAS_BASEMAP = False
    print("contextily not installed -- plotting without basemap.")
    print("Install with: pip install contextily")

gdf = gpd.read_file("auckland_cbd_buildings.geojson")
print(f"Loaded {len(gdf)} building outlines.")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

if HAS_BASEMAP:
    # Reproject to Web Mercator for basemap tile alignment
    gdf_wm = gdf.to_crs(epsg=3857)
    gdf_wm.plot(
        ax=ax,
        facecolor="tomato",
        edgecolor="darkred",
        linewidth=0.15,
        alpha=0.5,
    )
    cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.CartoDB.Positron, zoom=15)
    ax.set_axis_off()
else:
    gdf.plot(
        ax=ax,
        facecolor="steelblue",
        edgecolor="navy",
        linewidth=0.15,
        alpha=0.6,
    )
    ax.set_xlabel("Longitude")
    ax.set_ylabel("Latitude")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")

ax.set_title("Auckland City Centre Building Outlines (LINZ)", fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("auckland_cbd_buildings.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()



LINZ Export API
For the full national dataset, the Export API is the better option. The code is nearly identical to the Stats NZ version, with only the base URL and API key changed:

from config import LINZ_API_KEY

LAYER_ID = 101292
BASE_URL = "https://data.linz.govt.nz/services/api/v1"

HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"key {LINZ_API_KEY}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "crs": "EPSG:2193",
    "formats": {"vector": "application/x-ogc-gpkg"},
    "items": [{"item": f"{BASE_URL}/layers/{LAYER_ID}/"}],
}

response = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/exports/", json=payload, headers=HEADERS)
response.raise_for_status()

export_data = response.json()
export_url = export_data["url"]
print(f"Export job created: {export_url}")

# Poll and download using the same Stage 2 and Stage 3 code from Method A.
# Note: the full building outlines export may take several minutes and
# produce a file over 1 GB.

title: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
text:
Why Build a Dashboard?
In Part 2, you created choropleth maps showing urban indicators across Auckland. Those maps told a clear story, but they were static: users could not filter by time period, compare neighbourhoods side by side, or explore the data on their own.
A Shiny dashboard solves this. Instead of a fixed image, you give your audience an interactive tool where they can filter data by date or location, compare different scenarios, explore patterns through maps and charts, and access everything through a web browser without installing any software.

Week 8 (Polish and Deploy) focuses on finishing touches: advanced Shiny patterns, deployment with shinylive, interface design, and performance testing. By the end of this week, your dashboard should be live and publicly accessible.

title: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
section: What Shiny is, in one paragraph
text:
What Shiny is, in one paragraph
Shiny is a Python package from Posit (the company behind RStudio) that turns a Python script into a web app. You write the interface (a slider, a dropdown, a map) and the logic (what to do when the slider moves) in Python, and Shiny handles the HTML, the CSS, the JavaScript, and the browser communication for you. It started as an R package in 2012, and the Python version follows the same ideas.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
text:
Why “reactive”? A small thought experiment
Imagine a council planner opens your dashboard. They pick “Waitematā” from a dropdown. Three things should update at once: a map zooms to that local board, a table refills with its suburbs, and a chart redraws showing the age distribution.
In a normal Python script you would have to write, in order: “when the dropdown changes, rerun the map function, then the table function, then the chart function, and do not forget the one you added last month”. Every new output means another line of wiring. Miss one, and the dashboard lies to the user.
Shiny flips this around. You describe what each output depends on, and Shiny works out when to run it. If the map reads input.local_board(), Shiny quietly remembers that link. When the dropdown changes, anything that reads it reruns, and nothing else does. This style is called reactive programming, and it is the single idea that makes dashboards tractable.
You will feel this working in Section 3.1. The jargon can wait until 3.3.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python
section: The three parts of every Shiny app
text:
The three parts of every Shiny app
Every Shiny app, no matter how large, is built from three pieces:

The UI, a Python expression that describes what the user sees (inputs and outputs).
The server, a Python function that says how the outputs are computed from the inputs.
The App object, which glues the two together so Shiny can run it.

from shiny import App, ui, render

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.h2("Hello Shiny"),
    ui.input_slider("n", "Pick a number", 0, 100, 50),
    ui.output_text("echo"),
)

def server(input, output, session):
    @render.text
    def echo():
        return f"You picked {input.n()}"

app = App(app_ui, server)
That is a complete, runnable app. Move the slider in your browser and the text below it updates. You did not write any code to detect the slider change, or to refresh the text. Shiny noticed that echo reads input.n(), and that is enough.
We will unpack every line of this in 3.1.

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
text:
GTFS in one paragraph
The General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) is the standard format public transport agencies use to publish schedule data. A feed is a zip of CSV files: stops.txt, routes.txt, trips.txt, stop_times.txt, shapes.txt, plus a few others. For Auckland, the feed lives at Auckland Transport’s developer portal. For this section we will assume you have a copy in data/auckland_gtfs.zip.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
section: Loading a GTFS feed with gtfs_kit
text:
Loading a GTFS feed with gtfs_kit
gtfs_kit is a small Python library that handles the boilerplate of opening a feed, computing schedules, and producing GeoDataFrames.
uv add gtfs-kit
import gtfs_kit as gk

feed = gk.read_feed("data/auckland_gtfs.zip", dist_units="km")

print(f"Routes: {len(feed.routes)}")
print(f"Stops:  {len(feed.stops)}")
print(f"Trips:  {len(feed.trips)}")
Two operations you will use most:
# Geometry of every route as a GeoDataFrame
routes_gdf = feed.get_routes_gdf()

# Stops as a GeoDataFrame
stops_gdf = feed.get_stops_gdf()
For a Shiny app, save these once to GeoPackage (routes_gdf.to_file("routes.gpkg")) and load them at module level. GTFS parsing is too slow to do every time the app starts.

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
section: Treating the bus network as a graph
text:
Treating the bus network as a graph
Stops are nodes; route segments between consecutive stops are edges. NetworkX makes this straightforward:
import networkx as nx

def build_bus_graph(feed):
    G = nx.DiGraph()
    st = feed.stop_times.sort_values(["trip_id", "stop_sequence"])
    for trip_id, group in st.groupby("trip_id"):
        stops = group["stop_id"].tolist()
        for a, b in zip(stops[:-1], stops[1:]):
            if G.has_edge(a, b):
                G[a][b]["trips"] += 1
            else:
                G.add_edge(a, b, trips=1)
    return G
The trips attribute on each edge counts how many scheduled trips pass over that segment. High-trip edges are the trunk corridors (Dominion Rd, New North Rd, Great South Rd in Auckland). This is one cheap-and-cheerful proxy for “how important is this segment”.






Centrality measures, briefly





NetworkX gives you nx.betweenness_centrality(G), nx.closeness_centrality(G), and nx.degree_centrality(G). Each tells a different story about which stops are important. Betweenness flags transfer hubs; closeness flags accessibility; degree flags interchanges. Pick the one that matches your dashboard’s question, not all three.

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
section: Wrapping it in a Shiny app
text:
Wrapping it in a Shiny app
A small Shiny app for exploring routes by frequency:
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
from shinywidgets import output_widget, render_widget
from ipyleaflet import Map, GeoData
import geopandas as gpd

routes_gdf = gpd.read_file("data/auckland_routes.gpkg")  # precomputed

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider("min_trips", "Minimum daily trips",
                        0, int(routes_gdf["trips"].max()), 0, step=10),
        ui.input_select("route_type", "Route type",
                        choices=["All", "Bus", "Train", "Ferry"]),
    ),
    ui.card(
        ui.card_header("Auckland bus network"),
        output_widget("map"),
    ),
    title="AT route explorer",
)

def server(input, output, session):

    @reactive.calc
    def filtered():
        df = routes_gdf[routes_gdf["trips"] >= input.min_trips()]
        if input.route_type() != "All":
            df = df[df["route_type"] == input.route_type()]
        return df

    @render_widget
    def map():
        m = Map(center=(-36.85, 174.77), zoom=11)
        m.add_layer(GeoData(geo_dataframe=filtered(),
                            style={"color": "#d73027", "weight": 2}))
        return m

app = App(app_ui, server)
Same skeleton as 3.4. New bit: a real-world dataset and a meaningful filter (“how does the network look if I keep only routes with at least N trips a day?”). That kind of question is what makes a dashboard worth deploying.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
section: Common pitfalls with GTFS in shinylive
text:
Common pitfalls with GTFS in shinylive

File size. A full GTFS for Auckland is several MB. Aggregate to a daily summary (one row per route) before saving the GeoPackage.
Time of day. “Trips per day” hides peak-vs-off-peak. If your assignment is about congestion, slice by hour.
Direction. Stops are not symmetric; route shapes are directional. Check that you are not double-counting.
Holiday calendars. GTFS distinguishes weekday, Saturday, Sunday, and special services. Decide once which calendar you are using and stick to it.

title: 3.6. Bus Networks and Assignment 2
text:
Assignment 2 Brief
Due: Friday 8 May 2026 (end of Week 8), 23:59 NZST. Weight: 30% of the course mark. Format: a deployed shinylive URL plus a public GitHub repo.

What you must build
A Shiny dashboard that addresses one urban-analytics question about Auckland (or another New Zealand city, with permission). The question must be specific enough that someone could disagree with your answer.
Examples of acceptable questions:

“Which Auckland suburbs have the worst evening peak congestion, and how much would removing one lane on Dominion Rd change that?”
“How does bus accessibility to the city centre vary by suburb, and which areas are worst served?”
“Where in central Auckland are pedestrian volumes highest relative to footpath capacity?”
“Which neighbourhoods in the isthmus have the lowest green-space accessibility within a 15-minute walk?”



Required components
The dashboard must include all of the following.

Three or more pages built with ui.navset_tab or ui.page_navbar. Suggested split: Overview, Map, Data, About.
An interactive map with at least two user-controlled filters. ipyleaflet preferred (so it deploys to shinylive); folium is fine if you ship a traditional Shiny app.
A temporal or comparative element. Either a time-period filter (date range, hour-of-day) or a side-by-side comparison (two suburbs, two scenarios, before/after).
At least one reactive expression with @reactive.calc, shared between two or more outputs.
At least one @reactive.event or @reactive.effect doing something useful (a Reset button, a save-snapshot button, a “Recompute” gate on an expensive operation).
A polished UI using ui.page_sidebar, ui.card, and a shinyswatch theme.
Deployment to a public URL, either via shinylive on GitHub Pages, or a traditional Shiny deployment.
A README in the repo with: project description, data sources, how to run locally, deployed URL, and known limitations.



What we are looking for








Criterion
Weight
Notes




Question and framing
15%
Specific, answerable, defensible


Data and methods
25%
Clean inputs, sensible indicators, reproducible pipeline


Reactivity
20%
Correct use of calc/effect/event; no redundant computation


Map and visual design
20%
Readable, accessible, sensible colours, legend


Deployment
10%
Live URL, app loads in under 30 seconds first time


Documentation
10%
README explains what, why, how, and limits





Timeline







Week
Goal




6
Pick your question. Sketch the three pages on paper. Get a “hello world” Shiny app running.


7
Build the data pipeline. Get the map and at least one filter working. Push first commit.


8
Polish UI, deploy to shinylive, write the README, submit.





Submission
Submit a single PDF to Canvas containing:

The deployed URL.
The GitHub repo URL.
A 250-word abstract describing the question, data, and main finding.
Two screenshots: the Overview page and the Map page.







On data ethics



Anything you put into a shinylive bundle is downloaded by every user. Do not ship anything you would not put on a public website. If your data contains personal information, aggregate before bundling.

title: 3.1. Your First Shiny App
text:
Before you start
Install Shiny into your project environment. If you are using uv (from 1.2), run:
# Create and move into your shiny application directory
mkdir myapp
cd myapp

# Create a virtual environment, defaults to .venv
uv venv

# Activate the virtual environment
source .venv/bin/activate
# .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 # on Windows (PowerShell)

# Your prompt will prepend with the current directory name

# Install into venv
uv pip install shiny
You will also want the Shiny extension for Positron (or VS Code), which gives you a “Run Shiny App” button. Without it, you can still run an app from the terminal:
shiny run --reload app.py
The --reload flag restarts the app whenever you save the file. Very useful while learning.

title: 3.1. Your First Shiny App
text:
Step 1: Create an empty app
Make a new folder for this section and create a file called app.py. Paste the following into it:
from shiny import App, ui

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    "Hello, world!"
)

def server(input, output, session):
    pass

app = App(app_ui, server)
Run it. Your browser should open a blank page with the words “Hello, world!” in the top-left corner. That is already a complete Shiny app. Not a useful one, but a complete one.
Look closely at the shape of the file:

app_ui is an object describing what the user sees. Everything inside ui.page_fluid(...) appears on the page.
server is a function taking three arguments (input, output, session). For now it does nothing (pass).
app = App(app_ui, server) stitches the two together. Shiny looks for a variable called app when it starts.







Why page_fluid?



page_fluid makes the layout stretch to fill the browser window. There are other page layouts (page_sidebar, page_navbar) that we will meet in 3.4. For now, page_fluid is fine.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.1. Your First Shiny App
section: Step 2: Add a UI with inputs and outputs
text:
Step 2: Add a UI with inputs and outputs
Replace the body of app_ui so that it offers the user a choice of dataset and shows a summary and a table:
from shiny import App, ui, render
import pandas as pd

# Three small datasets to choose from
datasets = {
    "Auckland suburbs": pd.DataFrame({
        "name": ["Ponsonby", "Parnell", "Mt Eden", "Newmarket", "Grey Lynn"],
        "population": [12500, 8900, 15300, 11200, 14800],
        "median_age": [34, 42, 38, 41, 36],
    }),
    "Wellington suburbs": pd.DataFrame({
        "name": ["Kelburn", "Newtown", "Karori", "Thorndon"],
        "population": [4500, 9800, 15200, 3100],
        "median_age": [28, 35, 41, 44],
    }),
    "Christchurch suburbs": pd.DataFrame({
        "name": ["Riccarton", "Addington", "Sydenham", "Merivale"],
        "population": [8400, 5200, 6100, 3800],
        "median_age": [30, 33, 36, 48],
    }),
}

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_select("dataset", "Choose a dataset:", choices=list(datasets.keys())),
    ui.output_text_verbatim("summary"),
    ui.output_table("table"),
)

def server(input, output, session):
    pass

app = App(app_ui, server)
Save, and the page now shows a dropdown and… nothing else. The placeholders (output_text_verbatim, output_table) are waiting for the server to fill them in. Notice the pattern:

ui.input_*(id, label, ...) defines an input. The id is how the server refers to it.
ui.output_*(id) reserves a slot for an output. The server fills that slot with a function of the same name.

This naming convention (match an output_table("table") slot with a def table(): in the server) is the connective tissue of Shiny. Get it wrong and nothing renders. No error, just blank space. Check spelling first when things go missing.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.1. Your First Shiny App
text:
Step 3: Add server logic
Now make the outputs do something. Replace the server function:
def server(input, output, session):

    @render.text
    def summary():
        df = datasets[input.dataset()]
        return (
            f"{len(df)} rows, {df.shape[1]} columns\n"
            f"Mean population: {df['population'].mean():,.0f}\n"
            f"Mean median age: {df['median_age'].mean():.1f}"
        )

    @render.table
    def table():
        return datasets[input.dataset()]
Save, switch the dropdown, and both the summary and the table change. That is your first reactive app.
Walk through what just happened:

You pick “Wellington suburbs” in the dropdown.
input.dataset() now returns the string "Wellington suburbs".
Shiny noticed (silently, during the first render) that summary and table both read input.dataset().
Because the value they depend on changed, Shiny reruns both of them.
The page updates.

You did not write any “if the dropdown changed, update the table” code. You only declared the dependency by calling input.dataset() inside the output function. Shiny did the bookkeeping.






Parentheses matter



Inside the server, inputs are called as functions: input.dataset(), not input.dataset. Forgetting the parentheses is the single most common beginner mistake.
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.1. Your First Shiny App
text:
Step 4: Spot the duplication
Look at the two output functions. Both of them start with:
df = datasets[input.dataset()]
Right now that is fine. With three rows of data the cost is zero. But imagine this line was gpd.read_file("big_dataset.gpkg") and you had five outputs on the page. The file would be read five times, every time the dropdown moved. The app would freeze.
We need a way to do the work once and share the result with every output. That is what reactive.calc is for.

title: 3.4. Decorators and UI Polish
text:
Decorators, the practical list
Everything Shiny asks you to decorate falls into one of two buckets.
Reactive logic (@reactive.*):








Decorator
What it does
Use it when




@reactive.calc
Cached value, lazy
Two or more outputs share a computation


@reactive.effect
Side effect, eager
You need to log, write, or notify


@reactive.event(x)
Gate a calc or effect on an input
Button-triggered actions



Rendering outputs (@render.*):








Decorator
Output placeholder
Return type




@render.text
ui.output_text("id")
str


@render.text with ui.output_text_verbatim
ui.output_text_verbatim("id")
str (preserves newlines)


@render.table
ui.output_table("id")
pandas.DataFrame


@render.data_frame
ui.output_data_frame("id")
DataFrame or render.DataGrid (interactive)


@render.plot
ui.output_plot("id")
matplotlib Figure


@render.ui
ui.output_ui("id")
any ui.* expression


@render_widget (from shinywidgets)
output_widget("id")
an ipywidget (e.g. ipyleaflet Map)



A common beginner trap: @render.table gives a plain HTML table, which is fine but not sortable or scrollable. If you want a data grid, use @render.data_frame and return render.DataGrid(df, filters=True). Small difference, big UX improvement.

title: 3.4. Decorators and UI Polish
section: Giving your app a real layout
text:
Giving your app a real layout
Until now every app has been a flat ui.page_fluid: stack everything from top to bottom. That is fine for five lines, poor for fifty.

Sidebar layout
The default “dashboard” look is controls on the left, output on the right. One line:
app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select("city", "City", choices=[...]),
        ui.input_slider("min_pop", "Minimum population", 0, 20000, 0),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("chart"),
    ui.output_table("tbl"),
    title="Suburbs explorer",
)
The sidebar collapses on narrow screens; you get responsive design for free.


Tabs with ui.navset_tab
Multiple pages inside one app:
app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.navset_tab(
        ui.nav_panel("Overview",
            ui.output_text("summary"),
        ),
        ui.nav_panel("Map",
            output_widget("map"),
        ),
        ui.nav_panel("Data",
            ui.output_data_frame("tbl"),
        ),
    ),
)
For a top-of-page navigation bar instead (better for dashboards with three or more pages), use ui.page_navbar(...) at the outer level.


Cards
Cards are little boxed-off sections that group related content. They are the visual building block most modern dashboards use:
ui.layout_columns(
    ui.card(
        ui.card_header("Summary"),
        ui.output_text("summary"),
    ),
    ui.card(
        ui.card_header("Chart"),
        ui.output_plot("chart"),
    ),
    col_widths=[4, 8],
)
ui.layout_columns uses a 12-column grid (the same one Bootstrap uses). The col_widths argument controls how each child spans. For three equal columns, use [4, 4, 4].
crumbs: Part 3. Interactive Dashboards with Shiny for Python

title: 3.4. Decorators and UI Polish
text:
Themes
Shiny ships with Bootstrap under the hood, so you can swap the look by setting a theme. The easiest way uses shinyswatch (a small helper package):
uv add shinyswatch
import shinyswatch

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ...,
    theme=shinyswatch.theme.flatly,  # try: cosmo, journal, minty, darkly
)
Pick one that suits your dashboard and stick with it. Do not mix themes mid-app.
