title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Story problem
Why does GitHub keep refusing me?
You have followed Section 1.3, you have a GitHub account, you have installed GitHub Desktop, and your class343 project is sitting happily under version control. Then Lab 6 asks you to Publish repository in GitHub Desktop, and either nothing happens, the publish button spins forever, or you see a message like:
This is not a bug. GitHub refuses anonymous pushes, and since 2021 it no longer accepts your account password as a credential. Signing in to github.com in a browser is only half of it: GitHub Desktop also needs a valid credential for your account. The simplest way to provide one is a personal access token (PAT) that lasts the whole semester.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Authentication failed. Some common reasons include:
- You are not signed in to GitHub.com
- Your credentials have expired

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
What you will learn

Why GitHub needs a second form of authentication, even after you sign in to github.com in a browser
How to confirm you are logged in to the right GitHub account
How to create a fine-grained personal access token that lasts the full semester
How to sign in to GitHub Desktop with that token
What to do when things still go wrong







What about SSH keys?



SSH keys are the other supported method and are what most developers use day to day on the terminal. They are a bit more involved to set up (key generation, agents, ~/.ssh/config) and some university or corporate networks block outbound port 22, which breaks SSH entirely.
For this course we recommend a personal access token because it works everywhere, plays nicely with GitHub Desktop, and takes about five minutes. If you want to learn SSH later, GitHub has a good walkthrough: Connecting to GitHub with SSH.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Why this matters before Lab 6
Several labs in this course, starting with Lab 6, ask you to git push a local project to a new remote repository. GitHub Desktop’s “Sign in” step is only half the picture. Signing in tells the desktop app who you are, but when git itself (the program under the bonnet) talks to github.com, it needs its own credentials.
Students who rely on “I already logged in to GitHub in my browser” tend to discover this the hard way, often five minutes before a lab demo. Setting authentication up once, today, saves all of that.






Which method should I use?



Either works. Pick one and stick with it:

SSH key is the standard choice. Set it up once, and git push works silently forever.
HTTPS with a personal access token is easier on locked-down university or corporate laptops where SSH traffic is blocked. The token acts like a password you can revoke.

If in doubt, do SSH. Fall back to a PAT if your network blocks it.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Option 1: SSH key (recommended)

Step 1: Check whether you already have a key
Before generating a new one, check whether your laptop already has an SSH key sitting in the default location.

macOS / LinuxWindows


Open Terminal and run:
ls -al ~/.ssh
Look for files named id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub, or id_rsa and id_rsa.pub. If you see a matching pair, you already have a key and can skip to Step 3. If the directory does not exist or is empty, continue to Step 2.


Open Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) or PowerShell, and run:
ls ~/.ssh
or in PowerShell:
Get-ChildItem $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh
Same logic: a pair of id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub files means you already have a key. Skip to Step 3. Otherwise continue.





Step 2: Generate a new SSH key
Use the Ed25519 algorithm (modern, short, secure). Replace the email with the one attached to your GitHub account.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_github_email@example.com"
You will be asked three things:

File in which to save the key: press Enter to accept the default (~/.ssh/id_ed25519).
Passphrase: optional. A passphrase encrypts the private key on disk, so even if someone steals your laptop they cannot use the key without typing it. You can leave it empty for convenience, but a short passphrase is good practice.
Confirm passphrase: retype it, or press Enter if you left it blank.

You should now see two new files in ~/.ssh:

id_ed25519: the private key. Never share this. Never paste it anywhere.
id_ed25519.pub: the public key. This is the one you give to GitHub.



Step 3: Add the public key to GitHub
Copy the contents of the public key to your clipboard.

macOSWindows (Git Bash)Linux


pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub


clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub


cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Then select the whole line (starting ssh-ed25519 ...) and copy it manually.



Now register the key with GitHub:

Open github.com/settings/keys in your browser.
Click New SSH key.
Title: something memorable, e.g. UoA laptop (2026).
Key type: leave as Authentication Key.
Key: paste the clipboard contents into the big text box.
Click Add SSH key.

GitHub may ask you to confirm your password or a 2FA code before saving.


Step 4: Start the SSH agent and load the key
The SSH agent is a small helper that keeps your key ready in memory (so you do not retype the passphrase on every push).

macOSWindowsLinux


# Start the agent
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

# Tell macOS to store the passphrase in its Keychain
ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
If you left the passphrase blank, the ssh-add command just loads the key silently.


In PowerShell, enable and start the OpenSSH agent service (run PowerShell as Administrator the first time):
# One-off: enable the service
Get-Service ssh-agent | Set-Service -StartupType Automatic
Start-Service ssh-agent

# Add the key
ssh-add $env:USERPROFILE\.ssh\id_ed25519


eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519





Step 5: Test the connection
Run:
ssh -T git@github.com
The first time, SSH will warn you about an unknown host:
The authenticity of host 'github.com (140.82.x.x)' can't be established.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?
Type yes and press Enter. You should then see:
Hi <your-github-username>! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub
does not provide shell access.
That message is the success state. Your laptop can now push to any of your repos.






Use SSH URLs in your remote



After setting up SSH, make sure the origin remote uses the git@ form, not https://. Check with:
git remote -v
If it shows an https://... URL, switch it to SSH with:
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<your-username>/<your-repo>.git
Otherwise git push will still try to authenticate over HTTPS and ask for a password.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Option 2: HTTPS with a personal access token
text:
Option 2: HTTPS with a personal access token
If SSH is blocked on your network, or you just prefer HTTPS, you can authenticate with a personal access token (PAT). A PAT is a long random string that replaces your password on the command line. You can revoke it at any time from your GitHub settings.

Step 1: Generate a token

Go to github.com/settings/tokens?type=beta (fine-grained tokens, the modern option).
Click Generate new token.
Token name: something like UoA laptop (2026).
Expiration: 90 days is a sensible default for coursework. You can regenerate later.
Repository access: choose All repositories (simplest for the semester) or Only select repositories if you want tight scoping.
Permissions: under Repository permissions, set:

Contents: Read and write
Metadata: Read-only (set automatically)
Everything else can stay at No access.

Click Generate token, then copy the token immediately. GitHub will show it only once.







Treat the token like a password



Anyone with your PAT can push and pull from your repos as you. Do not paste it into chat, commit it to git, or share it over email. If you think it has leaked, revoke it from github.com/settings/tokens and generate a new one.




Step 2: Use HTTPS URLs
When cloning or setting the remote, use the https:// form:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo>.git
or, for an existing repo with an SSH remote:
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo>.git


Step 3: Cache the token so you do not retype it
The first time you git push, git will ask for a username (your GitHub username) and a password (paste the token, not your real password). After that, the OS credential helper stores it.

macOSWindowsLinux


macOS uses the Keychain automatically once you have Git 2.x installed. Just run:
git config --global credential.helper osxkeychain


Git for Windows ships with the Git Credential Manager. Enable it once:
git config --global credential.helper manager
The first push will open a browser window where you log in to GitHub; Credential Manager stores the token in the Windows Credential Vault after that.


Use the libsecret helper (GNOME Keyring / KWallet):
git config --global credential.helper /usr/share/doc/git/contrib/credential/libsecret/git-credential-libsecret
If that path does not exist on your distro, git config --global credential.helper store will cache the token in plain text in ~/.git-credentials. Use with caution.





Step 4: Test
Try a push to any of your repos. You should be prompted only the first time; after that, git pulls the token from the OS keychain silently.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
GitHub Desktop users
If you use GitHub Desktop rather than the terminal, you do not need to generate the token manually. The first time you push in GitHub Desktop, it opens a browser window, asks you to sign in to GitHub, and then stores its own token for you. That token lives in the same OS credential store and will be picked up by command line git too.
If GitHub Desktop fails to Publish repository in Lab 6, the most common causes are:

You are signed in to a different GitHub account in the app than in your browser (revisit Step 0).
The remote repo already exists and is not empty (see the callout in Lab 6).
Your university or workplace network is stripping HTTPS certificates (try a personal wifi or hotspot to isolate this).

Sign out of GitHub Desktop (File, Preferences, Accounts), sign back in, and try again before going deeper.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Troubleshooting

“Authentication failed” when I click Publish repository
Your stored credential has expired, been revoked, or never worked in the first place.

Check the token is still active at github.com/settings/tokens. If it has expired, generate a new one (Step 2) and sign back in (Step 3).
In GitHub Desktop, sign out of the account (Settings / Options -> Accounts -> Sign out), then sign in again.



The browser sign-in never completes
The browser opens, you click Authorize desktop, but GitHub Desktop does not register the login. This is usually a network or browser extension issue.

Try a different browser as the default (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari).
Disable any ad-blocker or privacy extension temporarily and retry.
Fall back to the token path in Step 3c.



GitHub Desktop keeps pushing as the wrong user
You have two accounts signed in, or the cached credential belongs to someone else. Sign out fully, clear any github.com entries from your OS credential store (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows), and sign in again with the correct account.


“Could not resolve host: github.com”
Not an auth problem, a network one. Check your wifi, try a different network, or check whether your university VPN is filtering DNS.


Publish repository says “already exists”
Not an auth problem either. The repository on GitHub already has content (often a README) that your local repo does not know about. See the Lab 6 callout on non-empty remotes.


I really need to use the terminal
Section 1.5 assumes GitHub Desktop. If you prefer the command line, GitHub’s guide walks through the credential helper setup in full: Caching your GitHub credentials in Git. The same token you generated in Step 2 works there.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Summary
You now know:

Why Publish repository needs its own authentication, even after you have signed in to GitHub.com in a browser
How to check you are on the correct GitHub account before you generate anything
How to create a fine-grained personal access token that lasts the whole semester
How to sign GitHub Desktop in with that token (browser path or token path)
How to diagnose the common failure modes

Key insight: do this once, and every lab afterwards (Lab 6, Lab 7, your Assignment 2 deployment) just works. Skip it, and you will spend lab time fighting Authentication failed instead of doing GIS.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Quick reference

One-time PAT + GitHub Desktop setup
0. Confirm you are signed in to the correct GitHub account in the browser.
1. Generate a classic token:
   https://github.com/settings/tokens
   Generate new token -> Generate new token (classic)
   Expiration: 90 days (covers the semester)
   Scope: tick `repo`
   Copy the token now (shown only once, starts with ghp_).
2. Open GitHub Desktop.
   macOS:   GitHub Desktop -> Settings -> Accounts -> Sign In
   Windows: File -> Options -> Accounts -> Sign In
3. Sign in using your browser -> Authorize desktop.
   (If that stalls, paste the token in the password field of the manual sign-in.)
4. Fetch origin on any repo. If it works silently, you are done.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Additional resources

GitHub Docs: Managing your personal access tokens – Creating a personal access token (classic) (the authoritative reference for this section)
GitHub Docs: Authenticating to GitHub in GitHub Desktop
GitHub Docs: Caching your GitHub credentials in Git (if you end up using the terminal later)
GitHub Docs: Connecting to GitHub with SSH (if you would rather use an SSH key)

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 0: Make sure you are logged in to GitHub
text:
Step 0: Make sure you are logged in to GitHub
Before you generate anything, confirm that your browser is signed in as the GitHub account you intend to push from. This sounds obvious, but many auth failures come from the laptop pushing as one user while the browser is logged in as another (often a personal vs. university account).

Open github.com in the browser you will use for the rest of this workflow.
Click your avatar in the top-right corner. Confirm the username shown is the one you signed up with in Section 1.3, using your University of Auckland email.
If it is the wrong account, sign out and sign back in as the correct one.
While you are there, click Your repositories and make sure you can see the repos you expect. If you cannot, you are signed in to the wrong account.

Keep this tab open. You will come back to it in Step 2.






Two-factor authentication



GitHub requires 2FA for most accounts now. If you have not set it up, do so before generating a token: Settings -> Password and authentication. You can use an authenticator app (recommended) or SMS. The token flow below assumes 2FA is enabled.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 1: Understand what a personal access token is
text:
Step 1: Understand what a personal access token is
A personal access token (PAT) is a long random string that acts as a scoped replacement for your password. A few properties worth knowing:

It belongs to you, not to a particular machine. The same token can be used on your laptop and your office desktop, or revoked from either.
You can limit which repositories it can touch and what it can do (read only, read + write, etc.).
It has an expiry date. When it expires, GitHub Desktop starts failing to push until you generate a new one.
If it leaks, you revoke it from a web page, not by changing your password.

GitHub offers two kinds of tokens:

Classic tokens (what we will use below). Scoped with a small set of permissions such as repo, which covers everything you need for this course.
Fine-grained tokens (newer). Let you restrict a token to specific repositories and individual permissions. Worth learning once you are comfortable, but overkill for a classroom workflow.

For the full reference on how tokens work, when to use which, and how to manage expiry, see the official GitHub docs: Managing your personal access tokens – Creating a personal access token (classic).

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 2: Generate a fine-grained personal access token
text:
Step 2: Generate a fine-grained personal access token

Still signed in to GitHub, open github.com/settings/tokens?type=beta.
Click Generate new token.
Token name: something you will recognise in six months, e.g. UoA laptop (2026).
Expiration: pick 90 days. This covers the remainder of the semester (including the Assignment 2 deadline on 10 May 2026 and any follow-up marking), so you will not need to regenerate before the course ends. If you prefer a fixed end date, use Custom and pick one just past the end of semester.
Description (optional): GISCI 343 course work.
Repository access: pick All repositories to keep things simple for the semester. If you prefer tighter scoping, pick Only select repositories and tick the gisci343-* repos.
Permissions, under Repository permissions:

Contents: Read and write
Metadata: Read-only (set automatically, required)
Leave everything else at No access.

Click Generate token.
GitHub shows the token exactly once, as a string starting github_pat_.... Copy it now into a secure place (a password manager if you have one). If you lose it, you will have to regenerate.

For reference, please visit https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens (screenshot below)







Treat the token like a password



Anyone with your PAT can push and pull from your repos as you. Do not paste it into chat, commit it to git, email it to yourself, or store it in a plain text file in your project folder. If you suspect it has leaked, revoke it immediately from github.com/settings/tokens and generate a new one.








Calendar reminder



Put a reminder in your calendar two weeks before the token expiry date. When it pops up, come back to this section and generate a new one. Future-you will thank present-you.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 3: Make sure your remote uses HTTPS
text:
Step 3: Make sure your remote uses HTTPS
Tokens authenticate HTTPS connections, not SSH. If your project has an SSH remote (starting git@github.com:), you need to switch it.
In your project folder:
git remote -v

If you see https://github.com/<username>/<repo>.git, you are ready. Skip to Step 4.
If you see git@github.com:<username>/<repo>.git, switch it:

git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo>.git
For a new project that does not have a remote yet, add one with the HTTPS form:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/<your-repo>.git

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 4: Enable the OS credential helper
text:
Step 4: Enable the OS credential helper
The first time you git push, git will ask for a username (your GitHub username) and a password (paste the token, not your real password). After that, the operating system caches the token so you do not retype it. Enable the helper once:

macOSWindowsLinux


macOS has a built-in Keychain. Tell git to use it:
git config --global credential.helper osxkeychain


Git for Windows ships with Git Credential Manager, which stores the token in the Windows Credential Vault and can even pop up a browser login on first use:
git config --global credential.helper manager


Use the libsecret helper (GNOME Keyring or KWallet, depending on your desktop):
git config --global credential.helper /usr/share/doc/git/contrib/credential/libsecret/git-credential-libsecret
If that path does not exist on your distro, a fallback is:
git config --global credential.helper store
This caches the token in plain text in ~/.git-credentials. Use only if you trust the machine.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
text:
Step 5: Push and test
Try a push from any repo you own (your class343 from Section 1.3 will do):
git push
You will be prompted:
Username for 'https://github.com': <your-github-username>
Password for 'https://<user>@github.com': <paste your PAT here>
Paste the token (it will not appear on screen, that is normal), press Enter. If everything is wired up, git pushes and the OS credential helper quietly stores the token. From now on, git push and git pull just work.
To confirm the token is stored:

macOSWindowsLinux


Open Keychain Access (Spotlight: Cmd + Space, type “Keychain”). Search for github.com. You should see an entry of kind Internet password with your GitHub username.


Open Credential Manager (Start menu search). Under Windows Credentials, look for an entry starting git:https://github.com.


Depends on your desktop. In GNOME: Passwords and Keys -> Login keyring -> search github.com.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 3: Sign in to GitHub Desktop with your token
text:
Step 3: Sign in to GitHub Desktop with your token
GitHub Desktop stores your credentials once and reuses them for every push afterwards. Do this once and Lab 6, Lab 7, and Assignment 2 will all just work.

3a. Open the accounts dialog

Open GitHub Desktop.
On macOS, go to GitHub Desktop -> Settings -> Accounts. On Windows, go to File -> Options -> Accounts.
If you see an existing account that is the wrong one (e.g. a personal account instead of your UoA one), click Sign out first.
Next to GitHub.com, click Sign In.



3b. Preferred path: sign in via your browser

In the sign-in dialog, click Sign in using your browser.
Your browser opens a GitHub page that says something like “GitHub Desktop would like permission to access your account”.
Make sure the account shown is the correct one (the username from Step 0). If not, click Not ? and switch.
Click Authorize desktop.
The browser hands control back to GitHub Desktop, which now shows your account under Accounts.

For most students on a home or campus network, this is all you need. Skip to Step 3d.


3c. Fallback path: sign in with your token
If the browser round-trip fails (common symptom: the browser opens, you click authorize, but GitHub Desktop stays on the sign-in screen), you can sign in directly with your PAT instead:

In the sign-in dialog, click the tab or link for Sign in using your username or email address.
Username: your GitHub username (the one from Step 0).
Password: paste the token you copied in Step 2 (not your GitHub password).
Click Sign in.

GitHub Desktop stores the token in your operating system’s secure credential store (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows). You will not be asked for it again until it expires.


3d. Verify
Back in the Accounts panel, you should now see your GitHub username, your avatar, and a green tick. Close the settings window.
Open (or reopen) any repository in GitHub Desktop and hit Fetch origin in the top bar. If the button spins for a second and then settles quietly, authentication is working.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 2: Generate a personal access token (classic)
text:
Step 2: Generate a personal access token (classic)

Still signed in to GitHub, open github.com/settings/tokens.
Click Generate new token, then Generate new token (classic). If GitHub asks you to confirm your password or a 2FA code, do so.
Note: something you will recognise in six months, e.g. UoA laptop (2026), GISCI 343.
Expiration: pick 90 days. This covers the remainder of the semester (including the Assignment 2 deadline on 10 May 2026 and any follow-up marking), so you will not need to regenerate before the course ends. If you prefer a fixed end date, use Custom and pick one just past the end of semester.
Select scopes: tick repo (the whole block: repo:status, repo_deployment, public_repo, repo:invite, security_events will all highlight). That is all you need for cloning, pushing and publishing repositories from GitHub Desktop. Leave every other scope unticked.
Click Generate token at the bottom of the page.
GitHub shows the token exactly once, as a string starting ghp_.... Copy it now into a secure place (a password manager if you have one). If you lose it, you will have to regenerate.

For reference, please visit https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens#creating-a-personal-access-token-classic (screenshot below)







Treat the token like a password



Anyone with your PAT can push and pull from your repos as you. Do not paste it into chat, commit it to git, email it to yourself, or store it in a plain text file in your project folder. If you suspect it has leaked, revoke it immediately from github.com/settings/tokens and generate a new one.








Calendar reminder



Put a reminder in your calendar two weeks before the token expiry date. When it pops up, come back to this section and generate a new one. Future-you will thank present-you.

title: 1.5 Authenticating with GitHub
section: Step 3: Sign in to GitHub Desktop
text:
Step 3: Sign in to GitHub Desktop
GitHub Desktop stores your credentials once and reuses them for every push afterwards. Do this once and Lab 6, Lab 7, and Assignment 2 will all just work.

Open GitHub Desktop. On macOS, go to GitHub Desktop -> Settings -> Accounts. On Windows, go to File -> Options -> Accounts. If a wrong account is already listed (e.g. a personal account instead of your UoA one), click Sign out first, then Sign In next to GitHub.com.
In the sign-in dialog, click Sign in using your browser.
Your browser opens a GitHub page that says something like “GitHub Desktop would like permission to access your account”. Make sure the account shown is the correct one (the username from Step 0). If it is not, click Not ? and switch.
Click Authorize desktop.
The browser hands control back to GitHub Desktop, which now shows your username and avatar under Accounts with a green tick. Close the settings window.

To verify, open (or reopen) any repository in GitHub Desktop and hit Fetch origin in the top bar. If the button spins for a second and then settles quietly, authentication is working.






If the browser round-trip fails



If the browser opens and you click Authorize desktop but GitHub Desktop stays stuck on the sign-in screen (rare, usually a locked-down network or an ad-blocker), you can sign in manually instead. In the sign-in dialog, choose the username and password option, put your GitHub username in the username field, and paste the token from Step 2 into the password field.
